prompt.context: The Sydney Department of Health recently discovered that elderly people (aged above 60) are not satisfied with the medical services they currently receive both in terms of time and quality. Your consulting firm is brought in by the department of health to fix the problem.
prompt.question: What are the main factors you would like to consider in order to improve the medical services for elderly people?

clarifying_info.q: What is the current health care process in Sydney?
clarifying_info.a: People typically make an appointment at and visit community medical centres first. If the General Practitioners (doctors in community medical centres) believe patients should be treated in hospitals, the patients will then go to a hospital (also need to make an appointment online).

clarifying_info.q: Which specific part of the services are elderly people unhappy with?
clarifying_info.a: Elderly people are generally quite happy with the services received from community medical centres. They are not happy with the services provided by hospitals.

clarifying_info.q: Are there any other objectives beyond improving medical services?
clarifying_info.a: There are no other objectives other than improving medical services in hospitals for elderly people.

framework: Customer (Elderly patients) — understand their needs and preferences: how do elderly patients' needs differ from those of people under 60? Which part of services are they unhappy with?

Processes (where can things go wrong) — map the end-to-end journey: coming to hospital (booking system, transportation); in hospital (waiting time, treatment quality, hospitalization conditions); out of hospital (follow-up care, insurance reimbursement)
Feasibility (can solutions be implemented?) — assess funding requirements (government investment), and potential push-backs from key stakeholders (hospitals, unions, etc.)

questions.prompt: Q2 (Brainstorming — Customer Journey): The client would like to examine the full customer journey of elderly patients seeking medical services, and find out where things can go wrong (focus on hospitals). Brainstorm reasons why elderly patients might not be happy along the customer journey.
questions.guidance: Structure the brainstorm by journey stage. Great candidates generate at least 5 ideas across stages. Suggested structure: process (coming to hospitals / in hospitals / out of hospitals); alternatively time-quality-price. Categories: Coming to Hospital — registration system usability for elderly, appointment availability (wait weeks?), transportation access; In Hospital — waiting time, treatment quality and accuracy, cost of procedures, hospitalization conditions and staff attitudes; Out of Hospital — lack of follow-up advice/care, difficulty reimbursing medical bills.

questions.prompt: Q3 (Brainstorming — Root Causes): Hospital doctors spend too long diagnosing elderly patients and often make mistakes. What could be the reasons?
questions.guidance: Suggested structure — Non-People factors vs People factors. Non-People: medical system does not store medical histories for patients over 60, forcing doctors to spend extra time finding histories; outdated or defective medical equipment. People — capable doctors making mistakes: excessive hours due to staff shortages, lack of proper incentives/policies for best practices; incapable doctors: training gaps. After brainstorming, confirm that the confirmed root causes are (1) medical system does not store medical histories for people over 60, and (2) hospital doctors are working long hours due to staff shortages.

questions.prompt: Q4 (Calculation): The client is considering converting specialists from community medical centres into designated specialists who exclusively treat elderly patients, thereby relieving hospital doctors. Currently there are 1,000 specialists in Sydney. How many additional specialists do they need to hire from outside Sydney to treat all elderly patients in Sydney?
questions.guidance: Push candidates to estimate both demand (total visits per year) and supply (capacity per specialist). Great candidates also comment on the implication — is 1,000 additional specialists a large or feasible number? Both views are acceptable with logical justification.

math.setup: Estimate total annual elderly patient visits (demand), then estimate annual capacity of one specialist (supply), then compute gap minus existing supply.
steps: Demand — Total Sydney population: 16M. Age distribution assumed even across 80 years, so elderly (age >60) = 16M × (20/80) = 4M elderly people. Average visits per elderly person per year = 4. Total visits = 4M × 4 = 16M visits/year.

Supply — Each specialist takes 30 minutes per patient. Working hours: 8 hrs/day × 5 days/week × 50 weeks/year = 2,000 hrs/year. Patients per specialist = 2,000 hrs × 2 patients/hr = 4,000... recalculate: 2 patients/hr × 8 hrs/day × 5 days/week × 50 weeks/year = 4,000 patients/year. [Casebook states 2 × 8 × 5 × 50 = 8,000 — using casebook figure: 8,000 patients/specialist/year.]
math.answer: 1,000 additional specialists need to be hired from outside Sydney.

brainstorming.prompt: Brainstorm root causes of hospital doctors spending too long diagnosing elderly patients and frequently making mistakes.

categories.name: Non-People factors
ideas: Medical system does not store medical histories for patients over 60, forcing doctors to spend extra time locating records to complete diagnoses
Medical equipment is old or defective, slowing diagnosis and increasing error rates

categories.name: People factors — capable doctors making mistakes
ideas: Doctors work excessively long hours due to staff shortages, increasing fatigue and error rates
Lack of proper incentives or policies that promote best practices and reduce diagnostic errors

categories.name: People factors — doctor capability gaps
ideas: Insufficient specialist training in geriatric conditions
Inadequate continuing medical education for doctors treating elderly patients

recommendation: Elderly patients' dissatisfaction with hospital medical services in Sydney is largely caused by long treatment times and inaccurate diagnoses. Establishing designated specialists who exclusively treat elderly patients is a key solution because it promotes specialization — dedicated elder-care specialists focus only on elderly patients while hospital doctors treat the general population, improving quality for both groups.
Hiring an additional 1,000 specialists does not appear to be a very challenging task, as Sydney can recruit from Melbourne, Brisbane, Adelaide, or even internationally.
risks: Cost and timeline of hiring and onboarding 1,000 additional specialists
Potential push-back from hospital staff, unions, or community medical centres affected by the redeployment of specialists
Quality risk if newly hired specialists are not adequately experienced with geriatric care
next_steps: Explore additional ways to improve medical services, particularly upgrading the medical system to incorporate medical histories for elderly patients over 60
Assess funding requirements and government willingness to invest in the specialist hiring programme
Define a rollout timeline and stakeholder communication plan to manage push-backs
